title: Adjusting with the seasons
hookLine: a rule bends for Advent, Lent, illness, busy years
tomorrow: why would a prophet write so a runner could read it?

lines: ISN'T A RULE THE SAME EVERY DAY?
cards: What happens to a rule when life breaks your routine? Start at noon, in a monastery, in summer. The brothers come in from the fields, sunburned, and eat together.
Then the bell doesn't call them back to work. The Rule of Saint Benedict tells them to lie down on their beds, in silence. Anyone who'd rather read may read quietly to himself.
A nap, written into a rule for monks. But isn't a rule supposed to be the same every day?

teach.h: A NAP, WRITTEN INTO THE RULE.
teach.b: Not Benedict's. His Rule sets one schedule for summer and another for winter, because the light and the work change.

In Lent it asks each monk to add something of his own: some extra prayer, some going without. For the sick it bends the furthest: care for them comes before everything, with food and rest the others don't get.
The old and the young get allowances too. The core stays: the prayer, the community, the work. The shape moves with the season.
Ecclesiastes says it in the Douay-Rheims: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven."
One to tell a friend: the Catechism says a serious reason, like illness or the care of an infant, excuses a Catholic from Sunday Mass.

Even the center of the week bends for a sick child. So a personal rule bends too: fuller in Advent and Lent, quieter in a brutal semester, very small in the year of a newborn or a diagnosis. Bending isn't quitting.
A rule that can't bend can snap in the first busy month, and then it's gone. A rule that bends is still there when the season turns.

how: Catholics often adjust their prayer and practices with the liturgical seasons, adding a sacrifice or extra prayer in Advent and Lent, and simplifying in illness, after a birth or in demanding stretches of life.

games.q: what does “adjusting with the seasons” mean?
o: keeping every practice identical, no matter what
giving up a practice whenever it gets hard
letting a rule of life change shape through the year

games.q: a rule that bends — tap the pairs.
p: rest on their beds after the meal
each adds something of his own

s: Benedict's Rule keeps one identical schedule all year round
it sets summer and winter hours, adds in Lent, and eases for the sick, the old and the young.
the Catechism says a serious reason like illness can excuse a Catholic from Sunday Mass
illness or the care of an infant, for example. even the center bends.

games.q: finals week. your rule says a daily rosary, and you're running on five hours of sleep. what bends, and what stays?
o: drop the whole rule until finals end, then start over fresh.
keep a smaller version: one decade instead of the whole rosary.
keep the full rosary and cut more sleep; the rule is the rule.
games.why: Benedict's Rule changes shape with the season and keeps its core. smaller, not gone: it bends, not breaks.

practice: Try wish, obstacle, plan. Wish: one practice from your rule you most want to keep. Obstacle: the season most likely to break it, like finals, a new job, a long illness.
Plan: the smaller version you'll do then, one decade instead of a rosary, one verse instead of a chapter.

wordCard.voice: Adjusting with the seasons. A rule that grows in Lent, shrinks in sickness, and keeps its core all year.

orig.note: Latin: all things have their season. the Vulgate's words in Ecclesiastes 3:1, behind the Douay-Rheims line.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: it bends, not breaks, like a monastery that naps in summer. Day 1744, done.

sources.q: All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2181 (excused for a serious reason, e.g. illness, the care of infants)
